recent_posts.title: 2026 State of Kubernetes Resource Optimization: CPU at 8%, Memory at 20%, and Getting Worse
recent_posts.summary: The 2026 State of Kubernetes Optimization Report reveals worsening resource utilization across tens of thousands of production clusters: CPU utilization dropped to 8% (from 10%), memory to 20% (from 23%), and GPU sits at just 5%. CPU overprovisioning jumped from 40% to 69% year-over-year. The report argues overprovisioning is structural — driven by padded resource requests, Helm chart conservatism, and lack of post-deployment review — and that it doesn't actually improve reliability. One case study showed OOM kills dropped to near zero after automated rightsizing cut provisioned CPUs by half. GPU economics are highlighted as especially problematic given rising prices (AWS raised H200 Capacity Block prices 15% in Jan 2026). GPU sharing via time-slicing and Spot instances can yield 70%+ savings. The key differentiator for organizations that closed the efficiency gap was continuous automated rightsizing rather than one-time or manual approaches.

recent_posts.title: Deploying GPU workload with Dynamic Resource Allocation
recent_posts.summary: Kubernetes 1.34 made Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) generally available, replacing the blunt `nvidia.com/gpu: 1` device plugin model with structured, attribute-based GPU requests. DRA introduces four core objects: ResourceSlice (describes available hardware), DeviceClass (groups devices), ResourceClaimTemplate (per-pod GPU requirements), and ResourceClaim (shared across pods). A practical walkthrough shows deploying a CUDA Mandelbrot fractal renderer with precise GPU requirements (Ampere architecture, 20+ GB memory), then scaling it using three GPU sharing strategies: time-slicing (sequential access), MPS (concurrent CUDA processes with configurable thread percentages), and MIG (hardware-level partitioning into up to seven isolated 1g.5gb slices on an A100). CAST AI's autoscaler integrates natively with DRA, reading ResourceClaims to provision the cheapest matching instance type automatically, including setting up MIG partitions.

recent_posts.title: Is There a Karpenter Equivalent on GKE?
recent_posts.summary: AWS and Azure have both adopted Karpenter for intelligent node provisioning (AKS reached GA in early 2026), but GKE still relies on Cluster Autoscaler, Node Auto-Provisioning, and ComputeClasses — none of which deliver Karpenter's just-in-time, single-node optimization model. Google's choice appears deliberate: keeping GKE operationally distinct reduces cloud portability and lock-in risk. The post walks through the limitations of each GKE autoscaling layer, explains why Autopilot's constraints matter for production engineering teams, and introduces Cast AI as a third-party controller that brings continuous node consolidation, rightsizing, and Spot VM management to GKE clusters without replacing existing infrastructure.

recent_posts.title: Meet OpsPilot: Your AI SRE Agent Built Into Cast AI
recent_posts.summary: OpsPilot is Cast AI's new AI assistant for Kubernetes operations, embedded directly in the Cast AI console. It connects to the same real-time data pipeline used for autoscaling and cost optimization, pulling cluster state, workload events, cost attribution, and audit logs. Instead of manually correlating kubectl output, cost dashboards, and event logs during incidents, engineers can ask natural-language questions and receive structured answers in seconds. It handles incident investigation (e.g., diagnosing CrashLoopBackOff with root cause and suggested fix), cost spike analysis, and policy configuration questions. Available now at no extra cost for all Cast AI customers, with RBAC-aware access controls.

recent_posts.title: Infrastructure Has a Closure Problem
recent_posts.summary: Infrastructure and operations teams are drowning in alerts, dashboards, and disconnected findings but lack a system to close the loop from detection to durable fix. Cast AI's Application Performance Automation (APA) is positioned as that missing layer — a runbook-driven system that correlates signals across cost, reliability, security, and runtime behavior, then carries issues through to resolution via pull requests, rollbacks, or direct automation. APA operates on a trust model where it starts with recommendations and earns autonomy over time, integrating with existing tools rather than replacing them. The post frames this as the natural next step after observability: not more visibility, but actual closure.

recent_posts.title: Scale AI workloads on any hardware with Cast AI support for TPUs
recent_posts.summary: Cast AI now supports automated provisioning and scale-to-zero for Google Cloud TPU v5e and v5p slices on GKE. Teams can treat TPUs as standard compute resources managed through a single control plane alongside CPUs, GPUs, and AWS Trainium/Neuron. The integration requires no additional device plugins — pod specs with standard node selectors and tolerations trigger automatic TPU slice provisioning. Current limitations include single-host slices only and GKE exclusivity at launch, with broader topology support planned throughout the year.

recent_posts.title: Tier Your Apps, Cut Your Costs: A Practical Framework for Spot Instances in Production
recent_posts.summary: Spot Instances can reduce cloud compute costs by up to 90%, but interruption risks often limit their use to non-production environments. This guide presents a tiering framework that categorizes applications by criticality (Tier 0-3) and assigns appropriate On-Demand/Spot instance mixes. Using Cast AI's Pod Mutations with Kubernetes labels, teams can automatically route workloads to suitable instance types while implementing guardrails like Pod Disruption Budgets, multi-replica deployments, and topology spread constraints to maintain reliability for critical services.

recent_posts.title: GPU Sharing, Now Native: Cast AI Adds DRA Support
recent_posts.summary: Cast AI now supports Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) for Kubernetes 1.34+ on GKE and EKS, enabling intent-based GPU allocation instead of hardcoded GPU counts. DRA allows workloads to reference resource claims that describe their needs, while Cast AI's Autoscaler automatically provisions the right nodes, selects instance types, and finds available capacity. The system integrates with existing GPU sharing strategies, applies Spot optimization with automatic on-demand fallback, and uses OMNI to expand capacity search across regions and clouds when local supply is constrained.

recent_posts.title: Why multi-cloud cost comparison requires vendor-neutral monitoring and automation
recent_posts.summary: Multi-cloud deployments offer flexibility but create significant cost management complexity. Comparing cloud provider pricing is challenging due to unclear cost implications, lack of visibility in pricing pages, and hidden variables like egress charges and inter-zone traffic. Vendor-neutral cost monitoring is essential for multi-cloud environments, providing granular resource tracking, cross-provider comparisons, and real-time visibility into spending patterns. Automation takes optimization further by continuously analyzing workloads, comparing resources across providers, and selecting optimal configurations without manual intervention. A case study shows how Flowcore achieved better cost visibility and automated optimization through dual-layer monitoring of both workloads and underlying infrastructure.

recent_posts.title: A Conversation with Benjamin Caouren on Why APA Makes Engineers More Essential, Not Less
recent_posts.summary: DevOps leader Benjamin Caouren shares his philosophy on Application Performance Automation (APA), arguing that automation elevates engineers rather than replacing them. He achieved 60% cost reduction in non-production environments using Spot Instances and automation, emphasizing that AI requires human oversight and context to work effectively. The key insight is that visibility into resource usage transforms teams from reactive firefighters to proactive architects. His approach follows a simple framework: do it, do it right, do it better. As systems become more autonomous, engineers who understand infrastructure fundamentals and business context become more essential, focusing on strategic decisions rather than maintenance tasks.
